intro: This is a list of over-the-counter medicines and tools for a family to keep at home for two weeks without a pharmacy. It counts packages, not doses: a child's dose goes by weight, so ask your pediatrician or pharmacist and write it on the medication list. Each line gives the age limit printed on its Drug Facts label.

rules.title: How much to keep
rules.text: Count packages, never doses. Keep the number of unopened packages each line gives, for each person in its age bands or for the household. The labels say to stop and ask a doctor if a fever lasts more than 3 days, so one package is meant for one illness; a second package covers a second person or a second illness in the same two weeks. The package counts are this site's assumption for a 14-day target, not an official figure. For prescription medicines, the American Academy of Pediatrics says to ask the pediatrician about a 2-week supply.

rules.title: Check the dates every six months
rules.text: Check the expiration date on each package every six months, and replace anything out of date or nearly so. FDA says there is no guarantee a medicine is safe and effective after its expiration date. Six months is this site's interval: FDA suggests a review at the new year or a spring clean, and MedlinePlus says to check regularly. Keep medicines in a cool, dry place such as a dresser drawer or kitchen cabinet, not a damp bathroom cabinet, as FDA advises.

rules.title: Lock it all away
rules.text: Keep all medicines up and away, out of children's sight and reach, and put it back after each use. Relock the child-resistant cap each time: the Academy says safety caps are child resistant, not child proof. Keep medicines in their original packaging, in a locked cabinet or container. Save Poison Help, 1-800-222-1222, in each phone: it is free, confidential and open all day, all year, anywhere in the United States. If a child swallows a medicine, do not make them vomit; call Poison Help.

hazards.title: No aspirin or bismuth subsalicylate for children and teenagers
hazards.text: Do not give aspirin, or bismuth subsalicylate (in some stomach and diarrhea medicines), to a child or teenager unless their doctor says to. Both labels say children and teenagers who have or are recovering from chickenpox or flu-like symptoms must not use them, because of Reye's syndrome. Check combination cold and pain medicines for aspirin too.

hazards.title: Never two medicines with acetaminophen
hazards.text: Do not give two products that both contain acetaminophen, such as a fever medicine and a cold medicine. FDA says this can lead to overdose, and each acetaminophen label says not to use it with any other drug containing acetaminophen. Read the active ingredients on each box before you give it.

hazards.title: No honey before age 1
hazards.text: Never give honey to a baby under 12 months, not even for a cough. CDC says honey can contain the bacteria that cause botulism.

hazards.title: Infants' ibuprofen drops are stronger
hazards.text: Infants' ibuprofen drops are twice as strong per milliliter as children's ibuprofen liquid (compare the strengths printed on the two labels and on the two lines below), so a dose written for one must never be given from the other. Write the product name and strength beside each child's dose.

hazards.title: Acetaminophen under 2 only with a doctor
hazards.text: Acetaminophen: not under 2 years without a doctor's guidance. Fever: a baby under 12 weeks with a fever is seen by a doctor before any medicine. The label says under 2 years, ask a doctor; the American Academy of Pediatrics says not to give it under 2 without a doctor's guidance, and that a fever in the first 12 weeks needs medical attention at once.

hazards.title: No ibuprofen under 6 months
hazards.text: Do not give ibuprofen to a baby under 6 months unless their doctor says to. The infants' drops label says under 6 months, ask a doctor.

hazards.title: No anti-diarrhea medicine for young children
hazards.text: The loperamide label says do not use under 2 and ask a doctor for ages 2 to 5. NIDDK says doctors typically recommend against over-the-counter diarrhea medicine for infants, toddlers and young children. Ask the doctor about oral rehydration solution instead.

hazards.title: No cough and cold medicine for young children
hazards.text: FDA does not recommend over-the-counter cough and cold medicine under 2, and makers label it do not use under 4. The American Academy of Pediatrics is stricter: from 4 to 6, only if the child's doctor recommends it.

hazards.title: No benzocaine or lidocaine teething gels
hazards.text: FDA says benzocaine or lidocaine rubbed on the gums for teething offers little or no benefit and carries serious risks; benzocaine can cause methemoglobinemia, which can be fatal. FDA points to the Academy's advice instead: rub the gums with a clean finger or give a firm rubber teething ring that is not frozen. The benzocaine gel under Mouth and teeth is for an older child's or adult's toothache only: its label says never for teething and do not use under 2.

hazards.title: Measure only with the device in the box
hazards.text: Measure each liquid with the syringe or cup that came in its own box; most labels say not to use any other device. Never use a kitchen spoon. If a medicine comes with no device, ask the pharmacist for one.

lines.purpose: for burning and irritation from dry eyes
lines.label_age: Label: no age limit given.
lines.note: The label says not if the solution changes color or turns cloudy, do not touch the tip to anything, and stop and ask a doctor for eye pain, changes in vision, continued redness, or if it lasts more than 72 hours.

qty.rule: One unopened bottle for the household. This site's assumption.

lines.purpose: for itchy eyes from pollen, grass, animal hair and dander
lines.label_age: Label: adults and children 3 years of age and older; children under 3 years of age, consult a doctor.
lines.note: An antihistamine eye drop. The label says not for contact lens irritation, take lenses out first and wait at least 10 minutes before putting them back, and stop and ask a doctor for eye pain, changes in vision, redness, or itching that gets worse or lasts more than 72 hours.

qty.rule: One unopened bottle for the household if anyone is aged 3 or over. This site's assumption.

lines.purpose: for a lost filling or a loose cap until you see a dentist
lines.note: CDC's travel health kit lists a temporary dental filling for lost fillings, newly painful cavities and broken teeth. Its maker says it is temporary, see a dentist as soon as possible, do not use it with throbbing pain or swelling, and it contains eugenol (clove oil). Follow the instructions on its package.

qty.rule: One unopened pack for the household if anyone is 14 or over. This site's assumption.

lines.label_age: Not a Drug Facts product: read the pack's own directions.

lines.purpose: for toothache pain
lines.label_age: Label: children under 2 years of age, do not use; children between 2 and 12 years of age, ask a doctor before use.
lines.note: For toothache only, never for teething: see the hazard on teething gels. FDA says benzocaine products should not be used for teething pain in children and can cause methemoglobinemia, which can be fatal. The label says stop and get medical help at once for pale, gray or blue skin, headache, a fast heartbeat, shortness of breath, dizziness or tiredness, and not for more than 7 days unless a dentist or doctor says so.

qty.rule: One unopened tube for the household if anyone is aged 12 or over. This site's assumption.

lines.purpose: for emergency treatment of an opioid overdose
lines.pack: one pack of 2 nasal spray devices
lines.label_age: Label: no age limit given. It is given to someone else.
lines.note: See X7-07 for where to keep it and the steps. CDC says it is sold over the counter, and you cannot use it on yourself, so tell others where it is. The label says call 911 right after the first dose and stay until the ambulance arrives.

qty.rule: Two packs for the household: one at home beside the first-aid kit and one in the grab bag (X7-07). Each pack holds two devices and stays whole, because the label says a second dose may be needed. This site's assumption.

lines.purpose: for taking a baby's or young child's temperature rectally
lines.alternatives: A forehead (temporal artery) thermometer: the Academy says it can be used at any age and is the next most accurate after rectal.
lines.note: The American Academy of Pediatrics says rectal is the most accurate, especially under 3 months, and to label the rectal thermometer so it is never used in the mouth. Never a mercury thermometer.

qty.rule: One for the household if anyone is under 6. This site's assumption.

lines.purpose: for taking temperature by mouth, from age 4
lines.note: The Academy says oral use from age 4. Keep it separate from the rectal one and label both. Never a mercury thermometer.

qty.rule: One for the household if anyone is aged 4 or over. This site's assumption.

lines.purpose: for measuring a liquid medicine that comes with no device
lines.pack: two syringes, one of each size
lines.note: A spare, for a medicine that comes with no device. The Academy says a syringe is the most accurate way to measure liquid medicine and the pharmacist can give you one. Where a label says use only its own syringe or cup, use that.

qty.rule: Two for the household if anyone is under 14. This site's assumption.

lines.ingredient: Each product's own syringe or dosing cup
lines.purpose: for measuring each liquid medicine
lines.pack: the one in each medicine's box
lines.note: Keep each device in the box of the medicine it came with, and never swap them between products or use a kitchen spoon. The labels say use only the enclosed device.

qty.rule: One per liquid medicine, kept in its own box. This follows the labels.

store_brand.text: FDA says a generic medicine has the same active ingredient, strength and dosage form as the brand-name medicine and works the same way. Before you buy a store brand in place of a brand named below, check that its Drug Facts panel lists the same active ingredient and strength.
